title: Teaching
text:
Teaching philosophy
I believe the goal of mathematical education is not to produce students who can execute procedures, but students who can think — who can sit with a problem they have never seen before and find a way in. In practice, this means I spend a lot of time asking questions rather than giving answers, and encouraging students to articulate why a method works rather than just that it works.
I am always happy to hear from students looking for support. Feel free to get in touch.

title: Welcome to my blog
text:
This is the first post on my blog, so it seems worth saying a few words about what this space is for.
I study mathematics. Most of what that means, day to day, is a lot of reading, working through proofs, getting stuck, going back, understanding something a little better than you did before. It’s a slow and private process, and there’s not much obvious output to show for it while it’s happening.
This blog is partly an attempt to make that process a little more visible, and partly a way of forcing myself to write. There is a certain kind of understanding you only arrive at when you try to explain something to someone else and I’m hoping this is useful for that.

title: Welcome to my blog
text:
What I’ll write about
A few things I have in mind:

Expository notes on mathematics I’m learning, definitions, theorems, examples, and the kind of context that textbooks sometimes skip.
Problems I find interesting, not necessarily hard ones, just ones where the solution surprised me or where I think the journey is worth documenting.
Reflections on studying, what’s working, what isn’t, and things I wish someone had told me earlier.

I’ll also write about my data science projects, books I’m reading, and anything interesting I come across.

title: Welcome to my blog
text:
A small example
To set the tone, here is a fact I find genuinely delightful. The sum of the first \(n\) odd numbers is always a perfect square:
\[
1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + (2n - 1) = n^2
\]
You can see why this is true without any algebra at all, you can just draw it:
■           (n = 1, sum = 1)

■ □
□ □         (n = 2, sum = 4)

■ □ □
□ □ □
□ □ □       (n = 3, sum = 9)
Each new odd number adds an L-shaped border to the previous square, and the result is always a square. That’s a beautiful proof.
This is the kind of thing I hope to write more of.
